question: Prediction of MCI-to-AD conversion (eventual conversion at any later visit) among ADNI MCI patients, from baseline cognitive scores plus hippocampal volume, APOE4 and demographics. P-178 restricts to early MCI and includes the scales used in ADNI diagnosis (ADAS13, ADAS11, FAQ, MMSE). P-212 includes all MCI and deliberately excludes those scales. Population subset and features are allowed differences.
metric: Accuracy with accuracy. P-212 reports no AUC.

figures.P-178: 9-feature random forest, 95 test patients, visit-level records. Accuracy 0.936, Wilson with n = 95 -> 0.868-0.970. Class-wise figures from Table 4: the majority-class SVC scores accuracy = precision = 0.900 with recall 1, so the test set is 90% non-converters. The RF's recall of 0.978 and precision of 0.952 then give converter sensitivity 0.556 and specificity 0.978, which reproduces the accuracy of 0.936. Balanced accuracy is 0.767 (subject-level SE with about 12/83 test patients: 0.5*sqrt(0.556*0.444/12 + 0.978*0.022/83) = 0.072 -> 0.626-0.908). At P-212's 46.8% converters these class-wise figures give 0.468(0.556) + 0.532(0.978) = 0.781.
figures.P-212: Held-out test set of 139 (74 sMCI/65 converters), stratified. RF: 92/139 = 0.662 (22 sMCI and 25 converters misclassified; specificity 0.703, sensitivity 0.615). Wilson: z^2/n = 0.0276, centre 0.658, half-width 0.078 -> 0.580-0.735. Balanced accuracy 0.659 (0.580-0.738). Ensemble: 95/139 = 0.683 (specificity 0.730, sensitivity 0.631), Wilson 0.602-0.755. Balanced accuracy 0.681 (SE 0.5*sqrt(0.631*0.369/65 + 0.730*0.270/74) = 0.040 -> 0.603-0.758). 50-fold CV on the 539 training subjects: RF 74.6% (Wilson 0.708-0.781), ensemble 74.9%.
figures.comparison: Raw accuracy: 0.936 lies far above both of P-212's held-out intervals, and 0.662 and 0.683 lie far below P-178's 0.868. After adjusting P-178 to P-212's class ratio, 0.781 (balanced 0.767) still lies above P-212's held-out intervals (0.735 and 0.755; balanced 0.738 and 0.758). P-212's figures lie inside P-178's wide subject-level balanced interval (0.626-0.908), so after adjustment the exclusion runs one way. The adjusted 0.781 sits on the upper bound of P-212's cross-validated interval (0.708-0.781).

matched_figure_check: No matched figure exists. Every P-178 model (6, 9 or 13 features) includes ADAS, MMSE and FAQ, and P-212 reports no model that includes them. Neither paper reports the other's population. P-178's class-wise figures show that its 90%-majority test set accounts for most of the raw gap: at P-212's class ratio P-178 would score 0.781 rather than 0.936. That narrows the gap from 0.27 to about 0.10, but the adjusted figure still lies outside P-212's held-out intervals, so prevalence is not shown to close it.
performance_validity: Passes as written: P-178's 0.936 accuracy and 0.96 AUC are below 0.97 on 383 patients, and P-212's figures are far below. P-178's design is optimistic in ways that are candidate explanations rather than the exclusion: visit-level records, random minority oversampling (Table 1 lists 402/402 testing records), and a feature group chosen by test accuracy. P-212 uses a stratified held-out test set of 139 subjects.

candidate_explanations.difference: Class prevalence: P-178's test set is 90% non-converters and P-212's is 47% converters. P-178's own figures show this accounts for about 0.16 of the 0.27 raw gap, not all of it.
candidate_explanations.quote: Support Vector 9-Features 0.900 0.900 1 0.948 0.54 (Table 4: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 Score, AUC)

candidate_explanations.difference: Circular predictors: P-178 includes the scales used to assign the diagnostic labels, and P-212 excludes them because they can inflate performance. P-212 names the mechanism but does not quantify it on its own data.
candidate_explanations.quote: scores from the neuropsychological tests used to define “ground truth” labels (i.e. stable or converters) were also included as predictors, which potentially could lead to inflated predictive performance due to circularity.

candidate_explanations.difference: Population: early MCI only, against all MCI with at least three visits and three MRIs.
candidate_explanations.quote: Early Mild Cognitive Impairment (EMCI) patients were eligible for our study as long as they had follow-up appointments for greater than a year.

candidate_explanations.difference: Evaluation unit and oversampling: visit-level records with minority oversampling, against one record per subject.
candidate_explanations.quote: Oversampling was then performed in order to balance the initially imbalanced classes prior to training the model with 1000 estimators.

candidate_explanations.difference: Feature group selected on test accuracy.
candidate_explanations.quote: While initially, using all 13-features seemed to provide the highest accuracy at 91.6%, we found that by removing the RAVLT features, our accuracy rose to 93.6% in the 9-feature group.

candidate_explanations.difference: Validation: a 95-patient random split, against a stratified 139-subject held-out test after 50-fold CV. P-212's own CV accuracy (74.6%) is higher than its test accuracy (66.2%).
candidate_explanations.quote: Our top performing RF classification had an average accuracy of 74.6% (mean across 50 cross-validation folds). When the model was evaluated on our unseen test set, the overall classification accuracy was 66.2%.

reason: Both papers predict eventual MCI-to-AD conversion in ADNI MCI from cognitive scores plus hippocampal volume and report accuracy. P-178's 0.936 (0.868-0.970) and P-212's held-out 0.662/0.683 (0.580-0.735/0.602-0.755) exclude each other, and neither is near ceiling. P-178's own class-wise figures show that its 90%-majority test set accounts for most of the gap. At P-212's class ratio P-178 would score about 0.78, which still lies outside P-212's held-out intervals, though only one way and at the edge of P-212's CV interval. The pair qualifies. The candidate explanations (prevalence, circular predictors, early-MCI population, visit-level oversampled evaluation, feature selection on test accuracy) are not shown to be sufficient together, and prevalence is shown to explain only part of the gap.
